# Model Architecture and Representation

Also called: Neural Radiance Field Representations, Implicit Scene Representations

## Overview
This article defines the neural [network architectures](#15530-network-architectures.md) and data structures used to represent 3D scenes in [differentiable volume rendering](#43-differentiable-volume-rendering.md) [G]. It solves the problem of mapping continuous 3D coordinates and viewing directions to radiance and density (or attenuation) values, enabling the synthesis of novel views from sparse or dense input imagery [G]. Unlike explicit voxel grids or mesh-based representations, these methods use coordinate-based networks (MLPs) or tensor decompositions to store scene information implicitly, allowing for high-frequency detail and differentiable optimization [G].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family share the core mechanism of querying a neural network with 3D spatial coordinates $\mathbf{x}$ and a viewing direction $\mathbf{d}$ to predict scene properties [G].
1. **Coordinate Query:** The input to the representation is a 3D point $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ [G]. In [standard NeRF](#979-nerf-volumetric-rendering-coarse-fine-sampling.md) variants, the viewing direction $\mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ is also included to model view-dependent effects (specularity) [G].
2. **Positional Encoding:** Raw coordinates are often mapped to higher dimensions using positional encoding $\gamma(\mathbf{x})$ to help the network learn high-frequency details [G].
3. **Neural Mapping:** A [Multi-Layer Perceptron](#23740-neural-network-for-transfer-function-parameterization.md) (MLP) or tensor factorization maps the encoded coordinates to:
    * Density $\sigma \in \mathbb{R}$ (or attenuation $\mu$) [G].
    * Color $\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ (or intensity $I$) [G].
4. **Volume Rendering:** The predicted values are integrated along rays using the [volume rendering equation](#2098-volume-rendering-equation.md) to produce pixel colors [G].

## Subtopics

### [PixelNeRF](7471-pixelnerf.md)
[PixelNeRF](#7471-pixelnerf.md) is a [neural radiance field](#834-neural-radiance-field-nerf.md) method that synthesizes novel views from one or a few input images by conditioning a standard NeRF renderer on image features extracted via a pretrained [CNN](#20776-2d-convolutional-neural-network-cnn.md). Unlike vanilla [NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md), which requires many views for training and relies solely on positional encoding, PixelNeRF projects camera rays onto the source image plane to extract spatial features for each query point, enabling sparse-view reconstruction. It differs from sibling methods like MVSNeRF by operating in view-space with direct ray-to-pixel feature extraction rather than canonical-space [voxelization](#12-voxelization.md).

### [Attenuation Field](9639-attenuation-field.md)
The [Attenuation Field](#9639-attenuation-field.md) method maps 3D coordinates $\mathbf{X}$ to attenuation coefficients $\mu$ rather than color values, modeling X-ray beam decay through diverse structures to a flat-panel detector. It solves transmission-based imaging reconstruction by adhering to the Beer–Lambert Law, differing from natural-image NeRFs that model emitted radiance.

### [TensoRF Training Configuration](18549-tensorf-training-configuration.md)
This configuration defines the [training protocol](#4528-training-protocol.md) for the [TensoRF representation](#3026-tensorf.md) in the context of sparse-view lung nodule volumetry from [digitally reconstructed radiographs](#1445-x-ray-simulation-via-ray-integration.md) (DRRs). It addresses the instability of standard TensoRF density parameterization, which causes zero gradient flow during early training, and introduces anatomy-aware regularization to prevent overfitting in highly under-constrained settings (18:1 parameter-to-ray ratio). It sets itself apart from standard NeRF variants by using vector-matrix (VM) tensor factorization for the density field and specific initialization shifts to ensure non-zero density gradients.

## Background
The concept of [Neural Radiance Fields](#4972-neural-radiance-fields.md) (NeRF) was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020 [G]. This work established the paradigm of using MLPs to represent continuous 3D scenes for novel view synthesis [G]. Subsequent works extended this to sparse-view settings by incorporating CNN-extracted features, as detailed in [PixelNeRF](7471-pixelnerf.md) [G]. The [Attenuation Field](9639-attenuation-field.md) approach adapts this implicit representation for medical X-ray imaging, replacing the radiance model with the Beer–Lambert law [G].
